title: Personal Agent Connector Manifest and Privilege Model (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a working sketch for a compact "personal-agent connector" manifest and an associated privilege model. The goal: define a minimal, auditable, and interoperable manifest format that third-party connectors (browser extensions, mobile helper apps, personal knowledge graphs, calendar integrators, etc.) can present to Redwood-hosted or private inference endpoints when a user installs or binds a connector to their personal agent instance.

Key goals / constraints:
- Least privilege: connectors should request precisely the capabilities they need (reads, writes, background-fetch, streaming, attachments).
- Human-readable consent (for UI) + machine-verifiable assertions (for runtime enforcement).
- Ephemeral delegation: capability grants should be short-lived and revocable without reissuing long-lived API keys.
- Auditability: every connector action must emit a minimal provenance record (who/what/when/capabilities-used).
- Offline-first friendliness: manifests should encode offline capabilities and a fallback policy for when Redwood cannot be reached.
- Small and extensible: manifest max ~4KB, structured but tolerant of unknown keys.

High-level flow (install + runtime):
1) Connector advertises manifest to user agent (browser/OS) or to Redwood console. The UI shows human-friendly name, vendor, requested capabilities with examples and suggested session TTL.
2) User approves via UI; the personal-agent runtime negotiates a capability token with Redwood (OAuth-like or signed JWT) describing granted scope and TTL.
3) Connector uses the token to call Redwood inference endpoints; Redwood enforces server-side capability checks and issues short-lived inner tokens if needed for backend-to-backend calls.
4) All calls include connector manifest id and the token; runtime attaches provenance header for tracing.
5) Revocation: user can revoke from console; runtime invalidates tokens and flags connector as disabled.

Manifest fields (compact JSON dictionary):
- manifest_id: stable connector identifier (uuid or did)
- name: user-facing name
- vendor: vendor or developer name + optional url
- version: semver-like string
- description: short plain text
- requested_capabilities: list of capability objects (see below)
- ui_hints: { icon_url, install_prompts } (only for display; not used for enforcement)
- background_policy: one of [always, only-with-foreground-consent, never] (fallback: never)
- data_policies: list of strings referencing privacy policies or short blurb
- sample_invocations: array of short natural-language examples that will be shown on consent screen
- contact_email: maintainer contact
- max_manifest_size: optional integer indicating compressed size limit expected

Capability object (flat):
- id: "read:calendar" or "write:notes" (namespace:capability)
- description: plain text explanation for user
- allowed_resources: list of resource selectors (e.g., "calendar:primary", "notes:collection:<id>") or ["*"]
- granted_by_default: boolean (false default)
- min_ttl_seconds: integer
- max_ttl_seconds: integer
- requires_mfa: boolean (server may require stronger auth for sensitive caps)

Design choices and rationale:
- Use namespaced capability strings for easier mapping to server-side enforcement and to reduce synonym collisions.
- allowed_resources is a simple selector language (not a full ACL). Selector is evaluated by the personal-agent runtime and validated server-side where possible.
- TTLs: allow connector to request ranges but final TTL is decided at grant time by policy. This keeps the manifest small while expressing intent.
- requires_mfa: useful for things like "send-email" or "initiate-payment" where UX flows differ.

Sample manifest (inline example, compacted into a single-line JSON string for the manifest blob stored with the connector registry):
{
  "manifest_id": "did:rdw:connector:7c9b2f14-e8a9-4d3a-9f2b-2f1a9e7c6b5e",
  "name": "Local Notes Sync",
  "vendor": "Indigo Labs (https://indigo.example)",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Syncs local notebook entries to the agent's private notes bucket.",
  "requested_capabilities": [
    {
      "id": "read:notes",
      "description": "Read users' private notes to perform merge/conflict resolution.",
      "allowed_resources": ["notes:collection:local-notes"],
      "granted_by_default": false,
      "min_ttl_seconds": 60,
      "max_ttl_seconds": 86400,
      "requires_mfa": false
    },
    {
      "id": "write:notes",
      "description": "Create/overwrite notes created by this connector.",
      "allowed_resources": ["notes:collection:local-notes"],
      "granted_by_default": false,
      "min_ttl_seconds": 60,
      "max_ttl_seconds": 3600,
      "requires_mfa": false
    }
  ],
  "ui_hints": {"icon_url": "https://indigo.example/icon.png", "install_prompts": ["Will sync notes every 10 minutes"]},
  "background_policy": "only-with-foreground-consent",
  "data_policies": ["https://indigo.example/privacy"],
  "sample_invocations": ["Sync local note 'Meeting A'"],
  "contact_email": "support@indigo.example"
}

Token and runtime enforcement model (sketch):
- After user consent, Redwood's auth service mints a signed capability token (CBT) with fields: connector_id, manifest_hash, granted_caps (list of id + resource selectors), issued_at, expires_at, session_nonce. Token is short-lived (default 1h) and rotated frequently.
- Connectors must present CBT in Authorization header. Personal-agent runtime should also attach a provenance header X-RDW-PROV: base64(signature of {token, local-runtime-id, timestamp}) to prevent token replay across runtimes.
- Server verifies token signature, checks manifest_hash against registry snapshot, ensures capabilities align with requested resources.

Provenance record minimum fields (for audit logs):
- timestamp
- connector_id / manifest_id
- user_id (subject)
- runtime_id (device or browser instance)
- invoked_capability_id
- resource_selector
- outcome (allowed|denied|error)
- request_size_tokens (if relevant)
- session_nonce

Revocation and policy changes:
- Manifest registry stores manifest_id->manifest_hash and metadata. If vendor updates manifest (new version), manifest_hash changes and existing tokens referencing old manifest are invalidated depending on policy.
- User-driven revocation: console sets connector state to disabled; auth service revokes active CBTs and adds connector_id to a short-lived denylist that is checked at auth time.

Edge cases and open questions (todo list):
- Offline connectors: how to make short-term offline grants secure without exposing long-lived keys? Consider COSE-signed offline grants with limited action list and one-time nonces stored in local secure enclave.
- Granular resource selectors: do we need a richer selector grammar for 3rd-party data stores? Tradeoff: expressiveness vs auditability.
- UX wording: map capability ids to plain-language examples (we need product copy help).
- Billing and cost signals: if a connector triggers high-cost model usage, how are alerts surfaced and who pays? Connectors should be able to include a cost-profile hint in the manifest to help user's agent warn.
- Cross-runtime token replay: ensure provenance binding includes runtime public key and that revocation is fast enough for interactive security needs.

Immediate next steps (practical checklist):
- Draft JSON Schema for the manifest and a compact example (put in repo under /specs/connector-manifest-v0.json).
- Implement a small validator in SDK (python + ts) that checks required fields and enforces max manifest size.
- Wire minimal consent UI in the local runtime to render sample_invocations + cost hint.
- Add a prototype CBT minting endpoint in auth service (internal PR next).

Notes to self:
- Keep manifest intentionally small; we can add extension blocks for highly specific vendors.
- Coordinate with security team on required fields for audit and KMS usage for signed artifacts.
- Run an internal tabletop for revocation flows with SRE to validate denylist performance.

End of sketch.

If anyone reading: please ping me (maya@redwood.ai) with edge-case scenarios or real connector examples you want supported; this is a personal working draft, so expect changes.
